title: How and When to Use a Dog Whistle | Dog Training Tips
summary: The dog whistle, invented in 1876 by Sir Francis Galton, emits a high-frequency sound (~35,000Hz) inaudible to humans but audible to dogs, making it a useful tool for training, especially for recall, barking control, and obedience. Its effectiveness depends on proper conditioning and association with commands, as the whistle alone is just an unconditioned stimulus. Overuse can desensitize dogs or cause discomfort. Training involves using the whistle to gain attention, followed by commands and positive reinforcement, gradually phasing out verbal cues. Dog whistles are favored for their distinct, discreet sound that travels long distances without disturbing humans or wildlife, commonly used in hunting, herding, and police dog training.

title: Chunking Strategies for LLM Applications | Pinecone
summary: Chunking is the process of breaking large text into smaller segments called chunks to optimize embedding and retrieval in LLM applications. Proper chunking ensures that embedding models fit data within their context windows and that chunks contain meaningful, searchable information. Fixed-size chunking is common, but content-aware methods like sentence splitting, document structure-based chunking, semantic chunking, and contextual chunking with LLMs can improve relevance. Choosing chunk size depends on data type, embedding model, query complexity, and application use case. Post-processing with chunk expansion can provide additional context during retrieval. Effective chunking balances performance, accuracy, and latency for applications such as semantic search, retrieval-augmented generation, and agentic workflows.

title: Memory in the Age of AI Agents: A Comprehensive Survey
summary: This comprehensive survey explores the evolving landscape of memory systems in AI agents powered by large language models (LLMs). It introduces a unified taxonomy of agent memory based on forms (token-level, parametric, latent), functions (factual, experiential, working), and dynamics (formation, evolution, retrieval). The survey distinguishes agent memory from related concepts such as LLM memory, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and context engineering, clarifying their overlaps and differences. Token-level memory is further categorized by topological complexity into flat (1D), planar (2D), and hierarchical (3D) structures, each with distinct organizational features and applications. Parametric memory includes internal (modifying base model weights) and external (using auxiliary modules) types, balancing adaptability and stability. Latent memory operates within internal model representations, categorized by generation, reuse, and transform mechanisms. The survey details advanced memory architectures including case-based, strategy-based, and skill-based memories, as well as hybrid systems integrating these types. Working memory mechanisms manage context actively within single and multi-turn interactions to enhance reasoning and goal alignment. Memory formation involves semantic summarization, knowledge distillation, structured construction, latent representation, and parametric internalization, while memory evolution encompasses consolidation, updating, and forgetting. The document reviews benchmarks, open-source frameworks, and emerging research frontiers such as automation-oriented memory design, reinforcement learning integration, multimodal and shared memory systems, and trustworthiness. It aims to provide a conceptual foundation for future agentic intelligence design and unify fragmented research in this rapidly expanding field.

title: End-to-End Test-Time Training for Long Context
summary: This paper introduces TTT-E2E, a method for long-context language modeling that formulates the problem as continual learning rather than architecture design. It uses a standard Transformer with sliding-window attention and continues learning at test time via next-token prediction, compressing context into model weights. The model's initialization is improved through meta-learning during training, making the method end-to-end both at test time and training time. Experiments show that TTT-E2E scales with context length similarly to full attention Transformers but with constant inference latency, making it significantly faster for very long contexts. The method outperforms other baselines in long-context language modeling tasks, though full attention still excels in tasks requiring detailed recall. The approach is connected to fast weights, meta-learning, and continual learning literature, and offers a new perspective on efficient long-context processing.

title: Hierarchical Labeling Techniques
summary: The document discusses effective hierarchical labeling strategies based on cognitive science, information architecture, and UX principles. It emphasizes using short, clear labels at higher levels of a hierarchy and progressively more detailed, source-linked descriptions at lower levels. Cognitive psychology identifies three abstraction levels: superordinate (very general), basic (default and most natural for users), and subordinate (fine-grained). Information architecture recommends organizing hierarchies with conceptual coherence at higher levels and specific constraints at lower levels, maintaining consistent semantics. Progressive disclosure is used to manage cognitive load by revealing information gradually, with top levels having brief labels and leaf levels containing detailed descriptions and document links. Neurological studies support designing hierarchies around diagnostic, high-information-gain splits. A practical design pattern includes ultra-compact superordinate categories aligned with user intent, basic-level human-default groupings with clear rules and descriptions, and subordinate levels adding discriminating features with verbose descriptions and explicit document links.
